intro: No European capital does ancient trees quite like London. Its oldest oaks survive largely thanks to royal appetite: kings walled off huge hunting parks for their deer, and the trees inside were left to grow old while the countryside around them was cleared. The city even gave its name to the London plane, the soot-proof hybrid that lines its streets. The trees here range from a churchyard yew older than Londinium itself to a plane once valued at three quarters of a million pounds. All but Kew are free, though two Temple trees keep lawyers' hours.
meta_description: London's ancient trees hide in royal parks and churchyards. Start with the Totteridge Yew, alive since before the Romans built Londinium.
question_answer: The oldest tree in London is the Totteridge Yew, a European yew in St Andrew's churchyard in Totteridge, North London, estimated at between 1,000 and 2,000 years old. It is the oldest living thing in the city, and it stands a 15 minute walk from Totteridge and Whetstone station on the Northern Line.
question_meta: The Totteridge Yew, up to 2,000 years old, is London's oldest tree. Where it stands, how to reach it, and the rest of the city's ancient trees.
question_context: Ring counting does not work on ancient yews because their heartwood rots away, so estimates for the Totteridge Yew run from 1,000 to 2,000 years. Even the cautious low end makes it older than any building in London, and the high end means it was already a substantial tree when the Romans founded Londinium. It stands in the churchyard of St Andrew's in Totteridge, a village long since swallowed by North London, and the 13th century church beside it is the newcomer on the plot: the tree predates it by centuries at minimum. The district's Hundred Court once met in its shade, which tells you how long it has been the local landmark. London's runners-up are oaks rather than yews: Richmond Park and Greenwich Park hold hollow pollards in the 700 to 900 year range, survivors of the royal hunting grounds. But for sheer age, nothing in the capital touches the yew. Getting there is simple: Totteridge and Whetstone station on the Northern Line, then a 15 minute walk through the old village.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in London?
faq.a: The Totteridge Yew in St Andrew's churchyard, Totteridge, estimated at between 1,000 and 2,000 years old. Even the cautious low estimate makes it older than any building in the city.

faq.q: Are London's ancient trees free to visit?
faq.a: All but one of the trees on this list are free: they stand in public parks, streets, churchyards and squares. The exception is the Old Lions of Kew, which need a Kew Gardens ticket.

faq.q: Why does London have so many ancient trees?
faq.a: Royal hunting parks. Kings walled off Richmond and Greenwich centuries ago, and the oaks inside were spared the clearing that transformed the surrounding countryside.
A hybrid plane tree that thrives on soot and hard pruning. London planted it everywhere from the 1700s on, and the tree took the city's name with it.

trees.name: The Totteridge Yew

location.address: St Andrew's Churchyard, Totteridge Village, London N20 8PR

trees.story: The oldest living thing in London stands in a churchyard most people drive straight past. This yew was already ancient when the Romans built Londinium two thousand years ago, and the church beside it is the newcomer: St Andrew's dates only to the 13th century, a good thousand years younger than the tree growing at its edge. A 2008 survey by the Conservation Foundation, the Ancient Yew Group and Barnet Council named it possibly the oldest tree in the city, though ring counting is useless here. Yew heartwood rots away long before it can be counted, which is why the estimate spans a thousand years, 1,000 to 2,000, rather than a single number. What survives is a hollow, propped trunk with a girth of nearly eight metres, kept alive the way most ancient yews are kept alive: repeated pollarding, cutting the tree back hard and often enough to reset its own clock rather than let it grow toward collapse. Totteridge was a village long before London reached it, and its Hundred Court, the local medieval assembly that settled disputes and collected dues, once met in the yew's shade, using the tree as a landmark centuries before anyone thought to measure its age.
trees.access: Free, open access, churchyard
trees.transport: 15 min walk from Totteridge & Whetstone station (Northern Line)

trees.name: The Royal Oak

location.address: Near Pen Ponds, Richmond Park, Richmond, London

trees.story: The wall came second. This oak was already centuries old when Charles I enclosed Richmond Park around it in 1637, walling off common land for his own deer rather than planting anything new. It has lived behind royal fences ever since. The tree is a massive hollow pollard now, its trunk split and gnarled into a shape wide enough to shelter a small football team, kept alive by the same repeated cutting-back that saves most ancient oaks from their own weight. Richmond Park holds one of the largest collections of ancient oaks in Europe, and the Royal Oak is treated as its figurehead: Sir David Attenborough chose it as the symbol of a conservation campaign for the park's veteran trees, and it carries its own entry in the Woodland Trust's national Ancient Tree Inventory, a formally surveyed and registered specimen rather than a folk legend. Fallow deer, descendants of the herd Charles I first enclosed the park to hunt, still graze in its shadow, close enough on a quiet afternoon that the oak and the animals read as one scene rather than two separate facts.
trees.access: Free. Richmond Park's pedestrian gates are open 24 hours a day, so the oak near Pen Ponds can be reached on foot at any time; vehicle gates 7am to 6:30pm.
trees.transport: Bus or car to Richmond Park, then on foot near Pen Ponds
trees.notes: Coordinates taken from the tree's own Woodland Trust Ancient Tree Inventory entry (ID 40404), grid reference TQ1938873126, converted from OSGB36 to WGS84. The ATI page carries no language obscuring or rounding this location (unlike some sensitive ATI entries), and the tree is a well-known, publicly signposted landmark, so the precise grid reference is used directly rather than the previous general "near Pen Ponds" estimate.

best_time.label: September to October: acorns drop, and a good mast year buries the ground in them

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the huge hollow pollard trunk, split and gnarled and wide enough to shelter a small football team. It stands near Pen Ponds in Richmond Park, usually with fallow deer grazing around it.

trees.name: The Cheapside Plane

location.address: Corner of Wood Street and Cheapside, City of London, EC2V 8AA

trees.story: The only Great Tree of London still standing inside the Square Mile grows out of a churchyard that no longer has a church. St Peter Cheap burned down in the Great Fire of 1666 and was never rebuilt, and the plane tree that replaced its congregation is old enough that nobody can say exactly when it was planted. By 1853 a cab company was advertising its rank simply as 'Under the tree, Cheapside,' proof the tree was already a fixed point on the map before street numbering caught up with London's growth. In 1901 the press went further and called it the most valuable tree in the world, a claim about the land beneath it as much as the tree itself. It has survived since through the Blitz, through the City's total postwar rebuilding, and through a peculiarity of property law. The leases on the buildings flanking it forbid construction above two storeys on that side, an accident of contract law that has kept its canopy open to the sky for longer than most buildings nearby have existed. William Wordsworth is thought to have had this exact tree in mind writing his 1800 poem Poor Susan, in which a countrywoman hears a thrush singing from a tree on Cheapside and briefly mistakes the City for home.

trees.transport: 2 min walk from St Paul's tube station

trees.name: The Berkeley Square Plane

location.address: Berkeley Square, Mayfair, London W1J 6EJ

trees.story: In 2008 a valuer put a price on one of the plane trees in Berkeley Square: 750,000 pounds, briefly the most valuable tree in Britain, a number that says more about Mayfair real estate than about the tree itself. The square's planes went into the ground in 1789, planted by the MP Edward Bouverie, who lived at number 13, and they now rank among the oldest London planes anywhere in the city. There are more than thirty of them, planted as a single scheme rather than one famous specimen, which is why this entry marks the square itself rather than a single trunk. The nightingale of the song 'A Nightingale Sang in Berkeley Square' almost certainly never existed as a literal bird here, nightingales do not really sing over central London traffic, but if one had, these are the branches it would have used. The planes were named among the original 41 Great Trees of London, and the Grade II listed garden they shade has kept the same rectangular shape since the square was laid out, a fixed green rectangle while Mayfair rebuilt itself around it for over two centuries.
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: 2 min walk from Green Park or Bond Street tube

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

This entry describes the square's plane trees collectively (30+ specimens, one individually named and valued); coordinates mark the square itself rather than one specific trunk among many, so location_precision stays approximate honestly.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by there being more than thirty of them, planted together in 1789 as one scheme, which is why this entry marks the square rather than a single trunk. It stands in the railed garden of Mayfair's Berkeley Square.

trees.name: The Sweet Chestnut of Greenwich Park

location.address: Greenwich Park, London SE10

trees.story: Charles II wanted Versailles and settled for Greenwich instead. After taking the throne in 1660, he ordered grand formal avenues cut through the old royal hunting park, hundreds of sweet chestnuts marched up the hill toward the future Royal Observatory in straight French rows. Most of that planting is gone, lost to storms, disease and three and a half centuries of ordinary attrition. This chestnut is one of roughly fifty survivors, and the one the Great Trees of London list points to in the Flower Garden. Its trunk has thickened into something closer to architecture than plant, and it has been pollarded more than once, a pruning technique that resets a tree's internal clock and is a large part of why it is still standing while so many of its neighbours from the same planting are not. Its slowly rotting heartwood, hollow in places, now shelters beetles and fungi that need old deadwood and nowhere else. Every October it drops a carpet of spiny green cases across the grass, food for the park's squirrels and for anyone willing to peel one open. It has stood through the Restoration, two world wars and the digging of anti-aircraft gun pits nearby. Unlike the oak that once stood a short walk from here, it has never stopped growing.
trees.access: Free. Greenwich Park's pedestrian gates are open 6am to 7pm (vehicle gates 7am to 7pm), as listed by The Royal Parks.
trees.transport: 10 min walk from Maze Hill station, into Greenwich Park

best_time.label: October, when its spiny nut cases carpet the ground beneath it

trees.name: The Mulberry of Charlton House

best_time.label: August, when it still fruits every summer despite four centuries of leaning

location.address: Charlton House, Charlton Road, London SE7 7TH

trees.story: James I wanted Britain to grow its own silk, and in 1608 he ordered mulberry trees planted across the country to feed the silkworms that would spin it. The plan collapsed almost immediately over a basic mistake: silkworms eat white mulberry leaves and mostly refuse black ones, and the trees planted nationwide, including this one, were black mulberries. Charlton House got one of them, and unlike England's silk industry, the tree itself survived the error by four hundred years and counting. It now leans so far from vertical that its lower branches nearly touch the ground, propped up by a scaffold of wooden supports rather than left to collapse under its own spread, and it still fruits every August, small dark berries falling onto grass that has replaced whatever formal garden once surrounded it. The tree predates the surrounding community centre by roughly three centuries. Charlton House itself, a Jacobean mansion finished the same decade this mulberry went into the ground, has changed use many times since, while the tree in its garden has simply kept growing, propped a little more with each passing century.
trees.access: Free, open grounds of Charlton House community centre
trees.transport: Charlton rail station, 5 min walk

trees.name: The Fulham Palace Oak

location.address: Fulham Palace Gardens, Bishop's Avenue, London SW6 6EA

trees.story: This oak survived five centuries partly because people kept attacking it. It was coppiced long ago, cut back hard to its base, a brutal-looking practice that paradoxically resets a tree's age clock and can add centuries to its life rather than shorten it. What grew back is a Holm Oak, an evergreen Mediterranean species that has no business thriving this far north, and quite possibly the oldest specimen of its kind anywhere in Britain. It grows in the grounds of Fulham Palace, for centuries the working home of the Bishop of London rather than a royal estate, and the two bishops most often credited with planting it, Edmund Grindal and John Aylmer, both lived here in the second half of the 16th century, among the first people in England to try growing the species at all. The oak was named among the original 41 trees given Great Tree status in 1988, and a later record corrected an old misidentification of the tree as a common Pedunculate Oak rather than the rarer Mediterranean evergreen it actually is. Fulham Palace Gardens are free to enter daily, which means reaching London's likely oldest holm oak costs nothing but the walk from Putney Bridge station.
trees.access: Free. Fulham Palace describes itself as open daily with free admission; its opening-times page lists the botanic garden as 07.00 to 18.00. Parts of the garden can close for private events. The oak stands at the south-east corner of the main lawn, near the Tudor wall of the walled garden.

trees.name: The Old Lions of Kew

location.address: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, Richmond, London TW9 3AE

trees.story: John Smith, Kew Gardens' first curator, gave five of its oldest trees a nickname that stuck, the Old Lions, veterans that have outlasted every curator, director and fashion in planting since the garden began. The group spans the site rather than clustering in one corner, with an oriental plane near the Orangery, an elm, a locust, and the most storied of the five, a Japanese pagoda tree planted in 1762 that ranks among the oldest of its species growing anywhere in Europe outside its native range. All five predate Kew's formal existence as a public institution. They were already growing when Princess Augusta laid out the first pleasure garden here in the 1750s, decades before Kew merged with the neighbouring Richmond estate and grew into the botanic garden it is today. Seeing all five in one visit means crossing a meaningful stretch of the grounds, since Smith grouped them by age and survival rather than by location, but each carries its own small marker naming it as one of the Lions. Entry to Kew requires a paid ticket, unlike most of London's ancient trees, but the garden built its reputation partly on outliving its own founders, and these five are the proof of it.

trees.name: The Evelyn Mulberry

best_time.label: August, when the fruit ripens, one of the few parts of Sayes Court's story that still repeats every year

location.address: Sayes Court Park, Sayes Court Street, Deptford, London SE8 5RA

trees.story: John Evelyn's garden at Sayes Court was one of the most celebrated in 17th century England, laid out by a writer and diarist who helped define English ideas about forestry and planting, and it lasted less than four decades before a tenant wrecked it for sport. Tsar Peter the Great of Russia rented the house in 1698 while studying shipbuilding nearby, and legend holds that he spent his evenings being wheeled through Evelyn's prized holly hedges in a wheelbarrow, flattening years of careful topiary for entertainment. Historians doubt Peter planted anything here himself, and this mulberry's own age is uncertain enough that the honest claim is only that it may have survived the same visit that ruined everything around it, not that it predates the destruction with certainty. What remains today is a fenced, propped tree standing in an unremarkable public park where almost nothing else of Evelyn's garden survives, plus a stone marker at its base that tells visitors the wheelbarrow story rather than leaving them to wonder why one old mulberry gets special treatment. It still fruits every August, one of the few parts of Sayes Court's story that still repeats on schedule rather than existing only in an old diary.

trees.transport: Deptford or Deptford Bridge station, 5 min walk

trees.name: Barney the Plane

location.address: Barn Elms, Rocks Lane, Barnes, London SW13

trees.story: The biggest London plane in the city is a tree most Londoners have never heard of. Nicknamed Barney, it stands at Barn Elms in the riverside suburb of Barnes, tucked at the edge of the land next to the London Wetland Centre, and it is old enough, over 300 years, that it is treated locally as potentially the single oldest London plane anywhere in the capital. The species is the city's signature tree for a reason. It tolerates soot, survives brutal pruning, and outlives almost everything planted around it, and Barney is the patriarch of them all in Barnes. Its own Great Trees of London plaque states the claim plainly, calling it simply the oldest in London, though the tree's coordinates only firmed up in 2026, when a photographer's geotagged shot of Barney was checked against the plaque's own recorded position and the two turned out to sit within nine metres of each other, close enough to count as the same tree rather than two separate estimates. Most visitors to Barn Elms come for the birdwatching at the Wetland Centre next door and walk straight past the small plaque without noticing it, which is itself part of Barney's story: London's biggest plane tree stands anonymously beside one of the city's most visited nature reserves.

trees.name: The St Paul's Churchyard Planes

location.address: North Churchyard, St Paul's Cathedral, City of London EC4M 8AD

trees.story:
Four planes stood on the north side of St Paul's churchyard until the Great Storm of 1987 took one of them down. The three that remain are, according to one detailed local history of the cathedral, over 250 years old, which would put their planting in the middle of the 18th century, when Wren's dome was still the newest thing on the skyline and the ground beneath them was a working burial place. That age comes from a single account. The London Parks and Gardens Trust inventory for the churchyard agrees only that these are among the oldest plane trees in the City, without giving a number or a date, so read 250 years as the best figure anyone has published rather than a measured one.

What they lived through is less disputed. On the night of 29 December 1940 incendiary bombs set the streets around the cathedral alight and burned out much of the City. The dome held, and so did the planes. Londoners later planted this species everywhere precisely because it shrugs off soot and smoke; these three were in the ground a century before that fashion started.

This is an ensemble rather than one specimen: three unnamed trees, none of them individually catalogued or given coordinates by any source. Stand on the paved path along the north side and all three are in one view. The pin marks that garden, not a particular trunk.
trees.access: Free, open access, public churchyard garden on the north side of St Paul's Cathedral (no ticket needed for the garden, only for the cathedral interior)
trees.transport: 2 min walk from St Paul's station (Central Line)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by there being three of them, a fourth having gone down in the 1987 storm. They stand in the north churchyard of St Paul's; from the paved path along that side all three are in one view.

trees.name: The Amwell Street Fig

location.address: Amwell Street, outside the former Clerkenwell Parochial Schools building, EC1R

trees.story:
This fig may have been planted as a teaching aid. It sprawls across the front of the former Clerkenwell Parochial Schools on Amwell Street, several stems rising from one rootstock and propped where the limbs have outgrown their own strength. Paul Wood, who has spent years cataloguing London's street trees, reckons it has stood here since the schools opened, put in deliberately at the front of the building and perhaps partly so that Bible lessons had something living to point at. Figs run all through scripture, and a fig outside the classroom window is an illustration nobody can lose.

The dates want care. The Amwell Society dates the school building to 1830, while other accounts say 1827. And the planting claim rests on that one specialist reading rather than on two independent records, so roughly 195 years is a careful estimate, not a birth certificate.

Clerkenwell changed around it more than most of London did: watchmakers, radical printers, the New River head a few streets north still delivering water into the city, charity schoolchildren giving way to board schools and then to flats. The building stopped being a school. The fig stayed, and Islington still counts it among the borough's notable street trees.

It is a working fruit tree on a public pavement in central London, which is the part that stops people. Come in late summer and the figs are there, at eye level, on the street.

best_time.label: late summer, when the figs ripen against the old school wall

trees.access: Free, open access, standing against a street frontage on public pavement
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Angel station (Northern Line) or Farringdon station
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the several stems rising from one rootstock and the props holding up the longest limbs. It stands against the front of the former Clerkenwell Parochial Schools building on Amwell Street.

trees.name: The Dorchester Plane

location.address: Forecourt of The Dorchester Hotel, 53 Park Lane, Mayfair, London W1K 1QA

trees.story:
One of the Great Trees of London stands at the front door of a hotel where a night costs more than most people's monthly rent, and you can walk up to it for nothing. The London Tree Forum and the Countryside Commission put this plane on their 1997 list of the capital's great trees, which was generous of them, since the Great Trees map dates its planting to the early 1930s, making it younger than almost every other tree on this page by a century or more.

The arithmetic is suggestive rather than proven. The Dorchester opened in 1931, and a plane put into a brand new Park Lane forecourt in the early 1930s fits that opening neatly, but no source actually joins the two facts, and the planting date itself comes from that one specialist record.

What the tree unquestionably has is roots. Its root plate has risen clear of the ground and spread across the forecourt in ridges, the sort of thing a city normally paves over and here has been designed around instead. The hotel's recent refit tucked its garden underneath the tree rather than the other way round.

It has stood through the Blitz, when the hotel's reinforced concrete frame earned a reputation for being bomb-proof and politicians and generals moved in for the duration, and through ninety years of Park Lane traffic since. You see it from the pavement. No need to go inside.
trees.access: Free, stands in The Dorchester Hotel's open forecourt directly on Park Lane, clearly visible and reachable from the public pavement without entering the hotel
trees.transport: 8 min walk from Hyde Park Corner station (Piccadilly Line)

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the roots, risen clear of the ground in ridges across the forecourt with the hotel's garden tucked underneath them. It stands on The Dorchester's forecourt on Park Lane, in view from the pavement.

trees.name: The Marylebone Elm

location.address: Pavement outside the Memorial Garden of Rest, 65 Marylebone High Street, Westminster, London W1U

trees.story:
Dutch elm disease killed around 25 million British elms from the 1960s on, roughly three quarters of the country's population. This one was missed. It stands on the pavement of Marylebone High Street, more than 100 feet of it by the Great Trees of London map, the last elm of its kind in Westminster to have escaped the beetle that carried the fungus through every hedgerow around it.

Specialist tree writers identify it as a Huntingdon Elm, a hybrid of wych and field elm. A recent account of the street calls it simply a wych elm, so the exact cultivar is not universally agreed. Nor is the age: writers through the 2010s consistently put it at about 150 years, which makes it roughly 160 now, a figure carried forward rather than measured.

It has outlived a church. The small garden beside it, the Memorial Garden of Rest, was laid out in 1951 on the site of the old St Marylebone parish church, which was bombed in the war and then demolished. The building is gone. The tree that grew outside it is still there, leaning out over the pavement as though it means to cross the road.

A naturalist photographed it in bud and healthy in 2017, and someone walking the High Street described it still standing there in April 2026.
trees.access: Free, stands on the open public pavement directly outside the small Garden of Rest, no restriction
trees.transport: 6 min walk from Baker Street station (Bakerloo, Circle, District, Hammersmith & City, Jubilee, Metropolitan Lines)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, more than 100 feet by the Great Trees map, and by the way it leans out over the pavement toward the road. It stands outside the Memorial Garden of Rest on Marylebone High Street.

trees.name: The Embankment Plane

location.address: North side of Horse Guards Avenue at the junction with Victoria Embankment, Westminster, London SW1A

trees.story:
The tree that helped make London a city of planes is not a London Plane. It is an Oriental Plane, one of the two species crossed to produce the hybrid now growing down half the streets in the capital, and it stands where Horse Guards Avenue meets the Victoria Embankment, on ground that was river water until Bazalgette's engineers pushed the Thames back in the 1860s.

The Great Trees of London map dates it to 1870 and gives the species. Both of those rest on that one specialist record. General histories of the Embankment agree that planes went in along the new road from about 1870, the first scheme in the city to plant a thoroughfare with trees systematically, but none of them names this individual tree. So it is a survivor of that first planting on the evidence available, rather than a documented one.

It has had a good view. Cleopatra's Needle was raised a few hundred metres along the same Embankment in 1878, trams came and went, the Ministry of Defence rose behind it in the 1950s, and Whitehall traffic has run past its trunk for a century and a half.

It gets called one of the tallest planes in Britain, a claim nobody appears to have checked. Easier to say what it plainly is, a very large tree on one of the busiest corners in Westminster that almost nobody stops for.
trees.access: Free, stands on the public pavement/verge at the Horse Guards Avenue and Victoria Embankment junction, fully open access, no restriction
trees.transport: 7 min walk from Westminster station (Circle, District, Jubilee Lines)

photo.attribution: Hopefully Acceptable Username, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the odd one out, an Oriental Plane rather than the London Planes on the streets around it, and by its size, one of the largest on that corner. It stands where Horse Guards Avenue meets the Embankment.

trees.name: The Great Plane of Brunswick Square

location.address: Brunswick Square Gardens, Bloomsbury, London WC1N 1AF

trees.story: This plane was planted for orphans. Brunswick Square Gardens was laid out in 1796 as green space for the children of the Foundling Hospital, and this tree is reckoned to date from that laying out, which makes it around 230 years old. Only the planes of Berkeley Square, put in seven years earlier, are commonly held to be older among the planes of central London. It has stood through everything Bloomsbury became, the Hospital selling up and moving out of London in the 1920s, its buildings coming down, the square rebuilt around the gap, the Blitz, and the concrete decks of the Brunswick Centre arriving to the west in the 1970s. The institution it was planted to shade is gone. The tree is not. In 2008 it was named one of the ten Great Trees of London, and it has since been given its own information board in the square, which is a quiet way of saying the neighbourhood knows what it has. Photographs taken in spring 2026 show it in full health. Neither source that agrees on the 1796 planting records a girth or a height, so there are no measurements to quote here, only the thing itself, a very large plane in a small square five minutes from Russell Square station, free and open, with the Foundling Museum on the far side telling the rest of the story.
trees.access: Free, open public garden square
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Russell Square station (Piccadilly Line)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the information board beside it and by its size, the one very large plane in a small square. It stands in Brunswick Square Gardens in Bloomsbury, with the Foundling Museum on the far side.

trees.name: The Valence Park Holm Oak

location.address: Valence Park, next to the moat at Valence House, Becontree, Dagenham, London RM8 3HT

trees.story: The October 1987 storm brought down some 15 million trees across southern England and left this one untouched. Its low, heavily buttressed frame is credited for that: a holm oak that grows outward rather than upward gives the wind nothing to lean on. Roughly ten years later it was added to the Great Trees of London list. How old it is depends on which source you take, and the two do not agree. The Barking and Dagenham Post, quoting the borough's own heritage education officer, credits the Mertinn family, German immigrants who had made their money in jewellery and bought the estate in the early 1700s, with planting it to make their grounds look grander. That would put it close to 350 years. The London Gardens Trust's survey record for the site is more clinical and dates the grounds' holm oak and yew only to the nineteenth century, which would make it under 225. Both agree on what stands there: one of the most impressive holm oaks in London, beside the moat of Valence House, a medieval manor that is now the borough's museum. One practical note. The moat enclosure immediately beside the tree was closed for restoration work due to finish in spring 2026, so whether you can currently get right up to the trunk is unconfirmed. The park around it stays open, and the pin here is park level rather than surveyed.
trees.access: Free, public park; the moat enclosure immediately beside the oak was closed for restoration works stated (2026) to complete by spring 2026, so current accessibility right up to the trunk is unconfirmed as of, though the wider park stays open
trees.transport: Becontree station (District Line) then bus 62 to Becontree Avenue/Valence Avenue, or Chadwell Heath rail station, roughly 20-25 min walk or a short bus ride either way
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the low, heavily buttressed frame, a holm oak grown outward rather than upward. It stands beside the moat of Valence House, the medieval manor that is now the borough museum.

trees.name: The Ravenscourt Park Baobab Plane
trees.age_estimate: roughly 100 to 200 years, exact age unknown

location.address: South of the lower grassy area, near the elm avenue, Ravenscourt Park, Hammersmith, London W6

trees.story: A virus is the best explanation anyone has for the shape of this tree. It carries a swollen, knobbled trunk under a crown far too small for it, the signature of the rare Baobab group of London plane, a form believed to come from viral infection rather than ordinary growth. Few are known; the closest comparable specimens grow in Canterbury. Nobody can say how old it is, and the sources sit far apart. A specialist plane blog puts its planting somewhere in the nineteenth century, so 150 to 225 years. A local tree firm reckons closer to 100, while allowing it might date to 1812, when the park was the private estate of George Scott. The same firm repeats a story that a wartime bomb damaged the tree and that the regrowth explains its shape; no other source carries it, so treat that as local legend until one does. What is documented is stranger. The arborist Richard Moore took cuttings from this exact tree. Two of six rooted and now grow at a sculpture park in Dorset, still far too young to show whether the swelling travels with the cutting or belongs only to the parent. It is one of two Great Trees of London inside Ravenscourt Park, standing south of the lower grassy area near the elm avenue, five minutes from the District Line station, and it is unmistakable once you are in front of it.
trees.access: Free, open public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Ravenscourt Park station (District Line)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the swollen, knobbled trunk under a crown far too small for it. It stands south of the lower grassy area in Ravenscourt Park, near the elm avenue, about 150 metres from the park's tree of heaven.

trees.name: The Fountain Court Mulberries

location.address: Fountain Court, Middle Temple, London EC4Y 9DH
location.neighbourhood: Temple, City of London / Westminster border

trees.story: Two black mulberries lean on wooden crutches either side of a fountain that has been running since 1681. They were planted for a queen's jubilee and the sources cannot agree which one. Middle Temple's own archive dates them to 1897 and Victoria's Diamond Jubilee. An independent mulberry history gives 20 June 1887, her Golden Jubilee, and adds that the planting was marked with a dinner in Middle Temple Hall. Ten years apart, both plausible, neither picked here: call the trees roughly 130 to 140 years old. Four went in together and only these two are left, the other pair removed in the 1970s. Black mulberry ages like this, going crooked and heavy limbed early, propping itself on whatever it is given, and fruiting hard regardless. Fountain Court is a small enclosed square between Middle Temple Hall and the gardens that run down toward the river, a working courtyard of the legal quarter rather than a park, and one of the quietest corners in the City. Access is real but narrow. The court and garden open to the public on weekdays, roughly 12:30 to 3pm, not on bank holidays, entered through the Garden Room off Middle Temple Lane, and they close in high winds or for private functions. Turn up inside that window and both trees are there, one on each side of the water.

best_time.label: August, when the black mulberries ripen and drop

trees.access: Genuinely public but restricted hours: Middle Temple's garden and Fountain Court are open to the public on weekdays roughly 12:30-3pm, excluding bank holidays, entered via the Garden Room off Middle Temple Lane; occasionally closed for high winds or private functions
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Temple station (Circle, District Lines)
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by the wooden crutches under their leaning limbs, one tree on each side of the water. They stand in Fountain Court, either side of the fountain that has been running since 1681.

trees.name: The Inner Temple Mulberry

location.address: Benchers' Walk, Inner Temple Garden, by the railings outside Paper Buildings, City of London EC4Y

trees.story: The Inner Temple's garden opens to the public for two and a half hours on weekday afternoons, and this tree is a fair reason to time the visit. A black mulberry stands by the railings of Benchers' Walk, outside Paper Buildings, its trunk about a metre and a half around and ten metres of crown above it. The Inner Temple's own history of the garden names it as one of the survivors of an old orchard, alongside a large-fruiting walnut and a quince, which is the institution itself calling this inherited planting rather than decoration. What no source will say is how old it is. There is no planting date anywhere, and black mulberries are among the hardest trees to age: they rot hollow early, lean until they need propping, and root wherever a low branch touches soil, so the trunk stops being a record of anything. This entry carries no age for that reason rather than a guess. The ground is famous for a scene that never happened here. Shakespeare set the plucking of the red and white roses, and with it the start of the Wars of the Roses, in the Temple garden; the tree is centuries younger than the fiction. Two hundred and fifty metres across the lane, Middle Temple's mulberries at Fountain Court at least have a disputed planting date to argue over. This one does not even have that.

best_time.label: August, when the mulberries ripen and stain whatever is underneath them

trees.access: Public, open weekdays 12:30pm-3:00pm only (not full daily access); the tree stands by the railings of Benchers Walk outside Paper Buildings
trees.transport: Temple station, 4 minute walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about a metre and a half round under ten metres of crown, an orchard survivor alongside a walnut and a quince. It stands by the railings of Benchers' Walk, outside Paper Buildings.

official_register.name: Morus Londinium London mulberry survey (Inner Temple Garden record)

trees.name: The Finsbury Circus Pagoda Tree

location.address: Finsbury Circus Gardens, City of London EC2M

trees.story: This is the only Japanese pagoda tree in the City of London, on the City of London's own account of its gardens, and a City business paper's tour of Finsbury Circus says the same. The species comes from China and flowers cream in August, when almost nothing else does, which is a useful habit in a garden ringed by offices where lunch happens outdoors. Both sources tie the tree to the garden's original 1815 layout by George Dance the Younger, and neither produces a planting record, so the age here is circumstantial: roughly two centuries, inferred from the design rather than read off a document. Treat it as a range rather than a birthday. It has come through the most disruptive stretch of its life. Finsbury Circus lost most of its surface to Crossrail works for over a decade, then closed in 2023 for the first full renovation of the gardens in more than a hundred years and reopened in May 2025. The gardens are small, 2.2 hectares, so finding it takes a minute. Half a kilometre south, the Cheapside Plane is the only Great Tree of London still standing inside the Square Mile, and Kew's Old Lions include pagoda trees of roughly the same generation in a botanical collection. This one has spent its two hundred years in the middle of the banking district instead.

best_time.label: August, when it flowers cream-white and almost nothing else in London does

trees.access: Free, public garden, standard park hours
trees.transport: Moorgate station, 3 minute walk; Liverpool Street station, 6 minute walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by being the only Japanese pagoda tree in the City, and in August by cream flowers when almost nothing else is out. It stands in Finsbury Circus Gardens, which are only 2.2 hectares.

trees.name: The Quaker Garden Planes

location.address: Quaker Gardens, between Banner Street and Chequer Street, Islington EC1Y

trees.story: George Fox, who founded the Quakers, was buried on this ground in 1691, and the plane trees standing over it are nowhere near old enough to have seen it. The burial ground took Quaker dead from 1661 until 1855, and the space became a public recreation ground in 1965, laid out inside the Banner Street estate with the trees left in place. Their age is genuinely disputed. Bunhill Fields Quaker Meeting's own account of the garden says the mature London planes here were planted about 1880, which makes them roughly 145 years old. A local record drawing on the London Gardens Trust inventory describes three notable planes, two of which may date from the 18th century, which would make them a century older and among the oldest planes in London. The two claims have not been reconciled, and this page follows the Meeting's own figure because it is the institution's own history, while saying plainly that the bigger claim is out there. It is worth not confusing this with the celebrated burial ground next door. Bunhill Fields holds Blake, Defoe and Bunyan and gets the visitors; the Quaker ground is a separate, quieter square of grass and trees between Banner Street and Chequer Street, six minutes from Old Street. The Amwell Street Fig is about 1.4 kilometres west if you want to make an afternoon of it.
trees.access: Free, public recreation ground (laid out 1965 within the GLC Banner Street estate), entered from Banner Street or Chequer Street
trees.transport: Old Street station, 6 minute walk
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them by there being three mature planes over a quiet square of grass, and by this not being the celebrated burial ground next door. They stand between Banner Street and Chequer Street.

trees.name: The Ravenscourt Park Tree of Heaven

location.address: Near the sports area and children's playground, Ravenscourt Park, Hammersmith W6

trees.story: Tree of heaven is the species councils spend money removing. This one has a plaque. The circular green plaque at its foot calls it one of the largest examples of the species in the country and one of the Great Trees of London, and the Tree Register's champion database carries it too, with at least one account calling it the tallest of its kind in Britain. Nobody gives it an age, and that absence is the interesting part. Ailanthus altissima arrived in Britain from China in the 18th century, spreads by seed and suckers, and is usually treated as short-lived, rarely making it much past fifty years. Something this size therefore breaks the pattern for its own species, and since no source anywhere offers a planting date, this entry gives no age rather than inventing one. It qualifies on size and status, not on years. It is also the cheapest addition to a walk on this whole list. The Ravenscourt Park Baobab Plane, with its swollen virus-knobbled trunk, stands about 150 metres away in the same park, which means Hammersmith now offers two Great Trees of London within a two minute walk of each other, near the sports area and the playground, five minutes from Ravenscourt Park station. The coordinates here come from the Great Trees map and are tree-level, so the pin lands on the trunk.
trees.access: Free, open public park
trees.transport: 5 min walk from Ravenscourt Park station (District Line)

trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the circular green plaque at its foot naming it a Great Tree of London and one of the largest of its species in the country. It stands by the sports area and playground in Ravenscourt Park.

trees.name: The Greenwich Park Shagbark Hickory

location.address: Flower Garden, Greenwich Park, London SE10

trees.access: Free. The Flower Garden is inside Greenwich Park, whose pedestrian gates are open 6am to 7pm (vehicle gates 7am to 7pm), as listed by The Royal Parks.
trees.transport: Maze Hill station or Greenwich DLR/rail, about 15 minutes' walk; same park as lon_005
trees.story:
Britain's largest shagbark hickory, by the reckoning of the Great Trees of London list, is an American nut tree just short of 100 feet tall, growing in the Flower Garden of Greenwich Park. The list named it one of the capital's Great Trees, and a tree-care firm's round-up of London's finest gives the same height. Nobody else has published a measurement, so treat the national title as the list's claim rather than a settled record.

The name describes the bark. On an old trunk it comes away in long shaggy strips that lift from the wood, which makes the tree look permanently half-undressed and is the quickest way to pick it out from its neighbours. The species belongs to the forests of eastern North America and reached Britain around 1629. This one is a long way from home and standing up well to it.

What this tree does not have is a birthday. No source dates it, and nobody has published its girth either. If you know when it went in, or have stood at it with a tape measure, tell us.

The pin comes from the Great Trees map rather than a survey of the trunk, so expect to look around the Flower Garden in the south-east of the park. Greenwich Park's old sweet chestnut is a short walk away, which makes this an easy second tree for the same afternoon.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its shaggy bark, coming away from the trunk in long strips, and by its height, just under 100 feet. It stands in the Flower Garden in the south-east of Greenwich Park.

trees.name: The Battersea Park Hybrid Strawberry Tree

location.address: near the south west corner of Ladies Pond, Battersea Park, London SW11

trees.access: Free; Battersea Park is a public park, open daily
trees.transport: Battersea Park rail station about 10 minutes' walk; Queenstown Road about 12
trees.story:
A round green plaque on the railings calls this the biggest hybrid strawberry tree in Britain, and dates the claim to 1997. Since then the titles have multiplied and drifted apart. A tree-care firm's survey calls it the largest in Britain by girth, just under 60 feet tall, and a Champion Tree of London. The Friends of Battersea Park, who know it best, settle for "second highest in the country" and "one of the treasures of the Park". They also call it the most splendid of the park's strawberry trees, which is the one title nobody contests.

It is a cross between the Mediterranean strawberry tree and its Greek cousin, and it shows off in two ways. The bark peels back to red, so the trunk looks freshly skinned all year, and it flowers in autumn, when most of the park is shutting down. The Great Trees of London list dates it to the 1850s. Where it came from, the Friends admit, nobody knows.

The last few years have been hard on it. A storm in February 2022 tore off a major limb, and in September 2023 the next bough up came down too. It is still standing, and still a Great Tree of London.

You will find it near the south-west corner of the Ladies Pond, ten minutes on foot from Battersea Park station, and the pin is on the tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the peeling red bark and the round green plaque on the railings naming it the biggest hybrid strawberry tree in Britain. It stands near the south-west corner of the Ladies Pond.

best_time.label: October and November, when it flowers while the rest of the park winds down

trees.name: The Brockwell Oak

location.address: Brockwell Park, Herne Hill, London SE24

verified_sources: https://lambethnews.wordpress.com/2008/11/19/wood-you-believe-it-two-lambeth-trees-in-londons-top-20/ (girth 'of over six metres'; 600 is a floor, not a measured figure)
trees.access: Free; Brockwell Park is a public park, open daily
trees.transport: Herne Hill station about 10 minutes' walk; Brixton about 20
trees.story:
The Brockwell Oak was old before Brockwell Park existed, and old before the country estate the park was made from. Lambeth Council, which owns the ground, said so in 2008 when the tree was counted among London's Great Trees, and put its age at probably well over 700 years. The Great Trees of London list is more cautious: 500 to 700 years as of 2010. Read together, they put the acorn in the ground no later than the early 1500s, and around 1300 or before if the council is right. That band is the honest answer.

Even at the cautious end it was more than a century and a half old when the Great Fire burned the City in 1666, a few miles to the north. The public, by contrast, are newcomers. The park only opened in 1892, when this oak was already several centuries into its life.

Lambeth gives its girth as over six metres. That is the council's figure rather than a published measurement, and it is a floor, not a ceiling. Photographs from May 2023 show it in full leaf, broad and heavy in open grass, with people picnicking in its shade.

The pin comes from the Great Trees map, not a survey of the trunk, so expect to look. You want an oak with a trunk over six metres round, standing in the open. It is not a subtle tree.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, which Lambeth Council puts at over six metres round, on a broad oak standing in open grass. It stands in Brockwell Park, ten minutes from Herne Hill station.

trees.name: The Dulwich Park Turkey Oak

location.address: south side of the south carriageway, Dulwich Park, London SE21

trees.access: Free; Dulwich Park is a public park (Southwark), open daily
trees.transport: North Dulwich or West Dulwich station about 15 minutes' walk; several buses to the park gates
trees.story:
Dulwich has exactly one Great Tree of London, and it is not a native oak. It is a Turkey oak, a southern European species, and it was among the original 41 trees chosen for the Great Trees list. The Dulwich Society, writing about the area's notable trees in 2020, called it perhaps the finest Turkey oak in Dulwich. The species has been planted in Britain since the early 18th century.

That date belongs to the species, not to this tree. Nobody has published when this one went in, how tall it is or how far round, and this page will not guess. If you know, or have measured it, tell us.

What it has instead is a plaque, set beside it to mark it as a Great Tree, and that is the most useful thing a visitor can know. Look for the broad, low crown near the south carriageway, the park's road on the south side, and then for the plaque at its foot.

The pin comes from the Great Trees map and lands close to where a photographer stood to take its picture in 2017, so it puts you within a few metres rather than on the trunk. Dulwich Park is free and open daily, about fifteen minutes on foot from North Dulwich or West Dulwich station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the plaque beside it naming it a Great Tree of London, the only one in Dulwich. It stands on the south side of the south carriageway in Dulwich Park, under a broad, low crown.

trees.name: The Carshalton Plane

location.address: Festival Walk beside the stream feeding Carshalton Ponds, Carshalton SM5

official_register.name: Forestry Commission remeasurement of 5 August 2026 with Sutton Council Parks Service (letter shown in the Secret Carshalton report); Great Trees of London list

trees.access: Free; stands beside the public Festival Walk by Carshalton Ponds, plaque at its foot (Geograph captions); no hours published, an open path
trees.transport: Carshalton station (Southern), roughly 10 minutes on foot (not source-stated; Carshalton Ponds are the landmark)
trees.story:
In 1964 the Forestry Commission set a plaque at the foot of this plane recording 123 feet, then the tallest London plane known in Britain. It has not stopped growing. On 5 August 2026 the Forestry Commission and Sutton Council's parks service measured it again: 39.6 metres tall, about 130 feet, and 7.6 metres round the trunk, almost 25 feet. Since the plaque, its girth has grown by 19 percent and its height by 6 percent.

The height record has moved on, though. On the Tree Register's list, as read by Secret Carshalton, the local site that published the new figures, two planes in Richmond stand at 40.40 and 40.25 metres. That makes Carshalton's the third tallest London plane on that list, still a giant and no longer the champion.

Nobody recorded when it was planted, and the guesses do not quite agree. The 1964 plaque already called it likely over 200 years old, which puts it past 250 now. The Great Trees of London list, which counted it among its original 41 trees, gave about 200 years as of 2010. Both are estimates rather than records.

It stands beside Festival Walk, on the stream that feeds Carshalton Ponds, with the plaque at its base and the Honeywood Museum a few dozen metres away. The path is open and free, and Carshalton station is roughly ten minutes on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the Forestry Commission plaque at its base and a trunk 7.6 metres round. It stands beside Festival Walk on the stream feeding Carshalton Ponds, a few dozen metres from the Honeywood Museum.

trees.name: The Gunnersbury Park Black Mulberry

location.address: Gunnersbury Park, below the terrace steps of the Large Mansion (Gunnersbury Park Museum), London W3

official_register.name: Morus Londinium London mulberry survey (Conservation Foundation), Gunnersbury Park record

trees.access: Free; Gunnersbury Park open daily 7am until dusk, museum Tue-Sun 10am-4.30pm, free entry (visitgunnersbury.org)
trees.transport: Acton Town station (Piccadilly/District) about 10 minutes to the park gate (official), South Ealing about 10 minutes to Popes Lane gate; Kew Bridge rail to the southern gate; then a walk to the Large Mansion

location_site.name: Terrace steps below the Large Mansion (Gunnersbury Park Museum)

trees.story:
This mulberry fell over and kept growing. At some date nobody recorded, the twin-stemmed tree below the terrace of Gunnersbury's Large Mansion keeled over. It now lies in a V shape, sending branches straight up to build a new, squat crown. Before it went down it stood about 11 metres tall, according to Morus Londinium, the London mulberry survey, which records a largest girth of 184 centimetres and classes the tree as Notable and recumbent.

Peter Coles of Morus Londinium found it on a visit in April 2024, tucked away near the foot of the steps that climb through an arch to the terrace, and reported it thriving. Its neighbour dwarfs it, a cedar of Lebanon over 200 years old. A young upright mulberry a few metres away seems to have died, so do not mistake that one for it.

The age is a single source's judgement: probably 19th century. The same writer suggests the Rothschilds planted it, which is an inference rather than a record; the family bought Gunnersbury in 1835. Somewhere between 150 and 220 years is as close as anyone can say.

The pin is the survey's grid reference, which lands near the steps rather than on the trunk, so let the cedar and the fallen V guide you. Black mulberries fruit in high summer, dark berries that stain whatever lies beneath. The park is free and open daily from 7am until dusk, about ten minutes on foot from Acton Town station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the twin trunk lying on the ground in a V, its branches growing straight up. It stands at the foot of the steps up to the Large Mansion terrace, beside a much larger cedar of Lebanon.

best_time.label: July and August, when the dark mulberries ripen and stain the ground

trees.name: The Marble Hill Black Walnut

location.address: Marble Hill Park, near the entrance from the Thames towpath, Richmond Road, Twickenham TW1

official_register.name: The Tree Register of the British Isles (champion record, measured by Owen Johnson 2001); Great Trees of London list

trees.access: Free: Marble Hill Park (English Heritage, open daily; park hours dawn to dusk, closing time varies by source, check English Heritage); the house is separate (Wed-Sun, seasonal, ticketed)
trees.transport: St Margarets or Twickenham rail station, roughly 15 to 20 minutes on foot (walk times estimated, not source-stated)
trees.story:
In 1907 the standard survey of British trees ranked this walnut first of its kind in the country. Elwes and Henry, in The Trees of Great Britain and Ireland, recorded it in 1905 at 98 feet tall with a trunk 14 feet 3 inches round. Owen Johnson of the Tree Register measured it again in 2001: 27 metres tall and 184 centimetres across the trunk, which works out at roughly 5.8 metres round. A century had taken a few metres off the top and added well over a metre to the waist.

The Tree Register's verdict, as quoted in John Grimshaw's garden diary, is that no other black walnut in England matches it for both height and girth with a full canopy. It was among the original 41 Great Trees of London.

Its age rests on a story. Tradition, repeated by Grimshaw, says Henrietta Howard planted it in the 1720s, and a London parks survey thinks it probably belongs to the park's original landscaping. Neither is a planting record, so roughly 300 years, somewhere between 250 and 320, is as close as anyone can honestly put it.

The pin comes from the Great Trees coordinate and is approximate. The park's own description puts the tree near the entrance from the Thames towpath, so start there. Marble Hill Park is free and open daily from dawn to dusk; the house is ticketed separately. St Margarets and Twickenham stations are each about 15 to 20 minutes on foot.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: a black walnut 27 metres tall with a trunk close to six metres round under a full canopy. It stands in Marble Hill Park near the entrance from the Thames towpath.

trees.name: The Osterley Park Cork Oak

location.address: north side of the lake, south of Osterley House, Osterley Park, Jersey Road, Isleworth TW7 4RB

trees.access: Osterley Park is a National Trust estate; the park is listed open 09:00 to 17:00 and the garden 10:00 to 17:00, with a charge for the garden and house and free entry for members. The National Trust page lists no charge for the parkland itself; check before going.
trees.transport: Osterley Underground station (Piccadilly line) about 10 to 15 minutes' walk to the park gate (not source-checked)
trees.story:
A Mediterranean oak has stood beside a lake in west London since, by the account everyone repeats, 1855. Cork oaks belong to Portugal and Spain, where their thick, spongy bark is stripped for bottle stoppers. This one has kept its bark, and its leaves too, because the species is evergreen, and the London Trees blog photographed it in full leaf in winter.

The Grafting Gardeners guide to London's greatest trees calls it one of the oldest and largest cork oaks in the country, and it was chosen as one of the Great Trees of London.

The date needs a caveat. The blog, the guide and the Great Trees list all give 1855, but they may be repeating one another rather than three separate records, so it is a date the tree is said to carry. If it holds, the oak is about 170 years old. Nobody has published its height or girth; if you have measured it, tell us.

It stands on the north side of the lake, directly south of Osterley House. This oak belongs to a variety that is barely older than it is. William Lucombe, a nurseryman in Exeter, raised the cross of a cork oak and a Turkey oak around 1763, and the hybrid still carries his name. Our sources are one chain, the Great Trees list and a guide drawing on it, so the age is a single estimate, somewhere between 200 and 260 years, and nobody has published a girth or height. trees.story:
Every Whitsun, until about 1825, the people of Harlington turned out to clip their churchyard yew into shape, and made a festival of it. Through the 18th and early 19th centuries the tree was famous for its topiary, and a print of it sits in the British Museum's collection. Then the shears stopped, and the yew went back to being a yew.

How old it is depends on whom you ask, and every answer is large. The church calls it at least 1,000 years old. A notice in 1914 said probably more than 1,000. The British Museum's record says over 900. None of those is a measurement, and old yews hollow out in a way that defeats ring counting, so the honest answer is a range rather than a number. The Ancient Yew Group measured it at 587 centimetres round at the ground and files it among the ancient trees.

It stands opposite the south door of St Peter and St Paul, and the church's own history says it may mark the spot where Christianity was first preached here. That is tradition rather than record, but it is an old tradition attached to an old tree.

The Ancient Yew Group also notes that Heathrow expansion plans could one day take the churchyard. For now it is free and open, about 1.5 kilometres from Hayes & Harlington station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size: the one great tree of the churchyard, 587 centimetres round at the ground. It stands opposite the south door of St Peter and St Paul.

trees.story:
On 20 May 1966 the Beatles spent the day among these cedars, filming the promotional clips for 'Paperback Writer' and 'Rain'. One of them, a cedar with a huge low limb, is known as the Beatles' cedar, and in 2025 it made the Woodland Trust's shortlist of ten for Tree of the Year. The band were late arrivals. The Chiswick House and Gardens Trust, which owns the gardens, dates its oldest trees to the late 1720s, when William Kent first worked on the garden, and says several came directly from Lebanon. Other accounts put the planting at 1720, 1726, 1741 or 1745, one of them saying the trees came from Sutton Court, so the honest age is roughly three centuries with a couple of decades either way. Today an avenue of them frames the house.

This entry is the group rather than one trunk. The cedars are spread across the grounds and our pin marks the gardens, not the Beatles tree itself. To find that one, go to the statue garden where the 1966 scenes were shot and look diagonally across for the low limb.

The Trust notes that its cedars can drop branches without warning, and the ground under the famous one is roped off. The gardens are open daily, from dawn to dusk.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise the Beatles' cedar by its huge low limb. It stands diagonally across from the statue garden where the 1966 films were shot, among the great cedars that frame the house's garden front.

trees.story:
Richmond Green is plane, lime and horse chestnut country, which is what makes this tree so easy to spot. On the Maids of Honour Row side, near the gatehouse of the old palace, a single stone pine holds up a flat, dark umbrella of a crown, the shape you know from Roman skylines and Italian hillsides, standing alone on an English village green.

It is one of the Great Trees of London, the list Trees for Cities keeps of the capital's remarkable trees, and it is the only tree of its kind on the green. The name comes from the terrace of Maids of Honour Row close by, though no source we have read explains how the pine came to carry it.

What we do not know is most of the rest. Nobody has published its age, a planting date or a girth, and we will not guess. If you know when it was planted, or have measured it, tell us.

It has had a rough year. Wikipedia's Great Trees of London list reports that the pine lost a major limb in August 2026. We have not seen the damage for ourselves, so read that as reported rather than confirmed; naturalists recorded the tree on the green in 2025. If you visit, tell us how it looks now.

trees.story:
In March 1604 the Percy family bought ten mulberry trees for Syon, and the purchase is still written down in their archives. Six more followed in 1645 and 1646. Morus Londinium, the survey of London's mulberries, reads those entries with care. If all ten of the first batch survived, it says, some of the trees here could be more than 416 years old.

That if matters. Nobody has dated an individual trunk, so the age here is an estimate from the purchase records, broad on purpose. What you can see is how these trees have aged. Old mulberries layer, their branches settling to the ground and rooting, and the orchard south-east of the house is now a set of multi-stemmed rings with the original central trunks almost gone. The tallest of the six stands about eight metres. Nineteenth-century writers were already describing a very old tree here with its branches down on the ground.

You may hear that the botanist William Turner planted a mulberry at Syon in 1548. The survey found no evidence of mulberries here that early, so treat that as a legend and the 1604 purchase as the record.

One more tree stands apart, alone in a fenced enclosure in the water meadow that the house's long gallery looks over, leaning and propped, probably once part of the same orchard. Syon's grounds are ticketed, so check the opening days before you go.

trees.story:
This oak has three names, and the sources disagree on which came first. It was the Cuckoo Oak, and it is also Bedford's Oak, after J T Bedford, the City of London councillor who fought in the 1870s to save the Forest. OpenStreetMap and the walking guides call it Grimston's Oak, after the cricketer Robert Grimston, who lived from 1816 to 1884. The Epping Forest Heritage Trust treats Bedford's and Grimston's as one and the same tree.

Whatever you call it, it has been a landmark for at least three centuries. An engraving from the 1870s shows it looking much as it does now, standing alone where several forest rides meet just north of Connaught Water. The Trust puts its age at possibly 400 years or more, and its girth at around five metres. Other guides say 350 years; one claims 750 years and a trunk over ten metres round, which sits badly with the Trust's own measurement.

The Trust is also honest about rank. At least twelve other oaks in the Forest are as large or larger. This one is not the biggest, just the one with a name, or three of them. Our source calls it simply an oak; it is most likely a pedunculate oak, the Forest's common species, but if you can tell from the acorns, tell us.

It is free and open at all times, about 25 minutes' walk across Chingford Plain from Chingford station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the wide oak, about five metres round, alone where several rides meet. It stands in Epping Forest just north of Connaught Water.

London Gardens Trust (via search summary, page 404s) lists three notable chestnuts (C17th-18th). Wanstead Wildlife says only a few large old trees remain from the Wanstead House avenues and calls the Bush Wood and George Green chestnuts the most significant. A Wikiwand copy of the Great Trees list says the tree survived arson attacks (hollow blocked with a wooden door); not seen on the primary page, so not stated. trees.story:
On 7 December 1993 one of the chestnuts on George Green was cut down for the M11 Link Road. Protesters had fought for it, and it had a nickname, the tree with a postcode. It was about 250 years old. Four of its neighbours are still standing, and a young chestnut planted in 1999 stands in as its replacement.

The survivors are old. The Great Trees of London guide says the George Green chestnut was probably planted in the early 1700s, and Wanstead Wildlife counts these trees, with those in nearby Bush Wood, as the most significant of the few large trees left from the avenues of Wanstead House. Other accounts stretch the age to about 400 years, so the honest answer is roughly three centuries, perhaps more.

Wanstead Wildlife measured all five in 2007 and 2008. The biggest is 6.0 metres round and 18.8 metres tall. Another, 3.9 metres round, is the tallest at 21.1 metres. A third is only half a trunk, after lightning struck it in 1984, and a fourth is an old pollard. Between them they have come through lightning and a road scheme, and they still stand on the green by the road junction.

The green is free and open at all times, five minutes' walk from Wanstead station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the four old sweet chestnuts on the green, the biggest about six metres round; the young one among them was planted in 1999. They stand on George Green, about 400 metres south of Wanstead station.

Lambeth Council (owner) calls it 'a large mature London Plane tree at its heart'. Brixton Buzz: in the centre of Brixton for 'around a hundred years' (no source given); survived the 1940 bomb strike that wiped out Brixton Theatre; the plot was Brixton Oval, garden laid out 1905, library built 1893, redesigned 1965-66 with the plane preserved as a central feature, paved over again in the mid-late 2000s redevelopment (Windrush Square). trees.story:
In 1940 a bomb destroyed the Brixton Theatre. The plane tree at the centre of what is now Windrush Square came through the same strike, and since then it has come through something almost as risky for a city tree, two redesigns of the ground around it.

The plot has a long paper trail. The plot was Brixton Oval, with the Tate Library built in 1893 and a garden laid out in 1905. In 1965 and 1966 the space was redesigned with the plane kept as its central feature. In the redevelopment of the late 2000s it was paved over once more, and the plane was kept once more. Lambeth Council, which looks after the square, describes it simply as the large mature London plane at its heart.

How old it is, nobody has pinned down. A local history piece says it has stood in the centre of Brixton for around a hundred years; a 2025 tree writer calls it Victorian and one of the finest planes in town. Somewhere past a century is as far as the sources go, and no one has published a girth. If you know more, tell us.

In 2008 it joined the Great Trees of London, named in a public poll of the city's twenty favourite trees. It stands alone in the middle of a paved square between the library and the Ritzy, free and open at all hours, five minutes from Brixton station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one huge plane standing alone at the heart of the paved square. It stands in Windrush Square, between the Tate Library and the Ritzy cinema.

trees.name: The Lewisham Elm

location.address: Ladywell Fields, riverside path, middle field, Lewisham SE13

trees.access: Free. Public park, open at all times.
trees.transport: Ladywell station (Southeastern), about 5 minutes' walk.
trees.recognise: On the riverside path in the middle field, just after the spiral bridge from the northern field, near the dawn redwood; the only tree in the park with its own sign.
trees.verify_notes: One of the original 41 Great Trees of London. Thought to be the only remaining specimen in Britain of the cultivar its plaque names, and one of very few mature elms left in London after Dutch elm disease (about 20 million English elms killed, Ladywell Live 4 Mar 2021). Species disputed: the council sign says Ulmus x hollandica 'Klemmer' (Flanders elm); Wikipedia's Great Trees list, citing the Tree Register, gives European white elm (Ulmus laevis), and the Ladywell Fields blog notes some experts think so too. Species written as European White Elm, flag. Ladywell Live: the mature tree could live another 200 years; two saplings grown from its seed (collected May 2018) were agreed for planting in the park. No girth, height or age on any fetched page. Pin from the Great Trees list coordinate 51.450645,-0.024501 (no OSM tree node there), approximate. Alive: iNaturalist observation 2026-05-29 within lifecheck radius (https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/366307628), Ladywell Live 2021. Two sources are local community sites, hence flagged. Photo candidate: Wikipedia list file 'Lewisham_Dutch_Elm.jpg'.
trees.story:
Dutch elm disease killed some 20 million English elms. This elm in a Lewisham park, which local reporting calls the borough's great survivor, is still standing. It is one of very few mature elms left in London, and if its plaque is right, it may be the last of its kind in Britain.

The plaque is where the argument starts. The council sign names it as a Flanders elm, Ulmus x hollandica 'Klemmer', and it is thought to be the only remaining specimen of that cultivar in Britain. The Tree Register, quoted on Wikipedia's Great Trees of London list, says it is something else, a European white elm, Ulmus laevis, and the Ladywell Fields tree walk notes that some experts agree. We list it as a European white elm and keep the question open. If you know elms well enough to settle it, tell us.

Whatever it is, it was one of the original 41 Great Trees of London, and it is the only tree in Ladywell Fields with a sign of its own. Nobody has published its age, height or girth. Local reporting in 2021 said the tree could live another 200 years. A local resident had grown two saplings from seed collected in May 2018, and the council agreed they could be planted in the park.

The park is free and open at all times, five minutes from Ladywell station. Follow the riverside path into the middle field.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its sign, the only tree in the park with one. It stands on the riverside path in the middle field, just past the spiral bridge from the northern field, near the dawn redwood.

Bromley Civic Society (10 Mar 2020): veteran Quercus robur, 'over 500 years old', reprieved when The Glades was built (1980s, centre opened 1991), originally on the corner of the grounds of Bromley Lodge and Love Lane, now stands at the side of Kentish Way. trees.story:
When Bromley built The Glades shopping centre in the 1980s, this oak was reprieved. It now stands beside Kentish Way, a veteran on the grass at the edge of a mall that opened in 1991.

It was here long before any of that. The Bromley Civic Society says the oak first stood on the corner of the grounds of Bromley Lodge, where they met Love Lane.

How long it has stood there is disputed. The Civic Society calls it over 500 years old; the 2010 Time Out guide to the Great Trees of London says about 400. Neither figure comes with a measurement behind it, and nobody has published a girth or a height, so read it as somewhere between four and five centuries and more than a little uncertain. If you have measured it, tell us.

It is one of the original 41 Great Trees of London, chosen when the list was first drawn up, and it is a strange thing to meet among the shoppers. If the Civic Society is right, it was already growing before Henry VIII broke with Rome. Recent reports of it are thin. If you pass it, tell us how it looks.

It is free to see from the pavement, eight minutes' walk from Bromley North station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the lone veteran oak on the grass beside the road. It stands beside Kentish Way, on the edge of The Glades shopping centre grounds.

Exploring London 2024: 'visibly deteriorating' in 2017, geo-injector soil decompaction treatment that extended its life. Fenced (one source says enclosed to protect its root system). trees.story:
On 30 September 1937 Bexley became a borough under this oak. Lord Cornwallis presented the charter beneath its branches in Danson Park, hence the name. The borough's coat of arms carries an oak too.

Eighty years later it needed help. By 2017 the tree was visibly deteriorating, and it was given a soil treatment, decompacting the ground around its roots with a geo-injector, which by one account extended its life. Today it stands inside a fence that keeps people off the root zone, and it is seen from outside that fence.

The fence has a side effect. When a Kent heritage tree survey came through in 2015, nobody could get close enough to measure the girth, so there is no published figure. The age is loose as well. The 2010 Time Out guide to the Great Trees of London says well over 200 years; a 2024 history piece says around 200. Two centuries or a little more is the honest reading.

It was one of the original 41 Great Trees of London. OpenStreetMap mappers were still updating its record in April 2025, which is the most recent sign we have that it stands. If you visit, tell us how it looks.

Danson Park is free and open at all times, about 20 to 25 minutes' walk from Bexleyheath or Welling station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its fence, the big oak standing in its own enclosure out in the open parkland. It stands in Danson Park, Bexleyheath.

trees.story:
When a mapper from Trees for Cities put this chestnut on OpenStreetMap, the start date they gave it was simply 'before 1700'. It was one of the original 41 Great Trees of London, the list that charity drew up of the capital's remarkable trees, and it stands at the Ashcombe Road edge of Carshalton Park.

It is not alone. Carshalton Park holds a collection of veteran sweet chestnuts that Greenspace Information for Greater London counts as significant for the whole borough, and about 60 metres from this one stands a second Great Tree, the Carshalton Park Sweet Chestnut. That neighbour is the one with the hollow. Time Out's 2010 guide says it is around 400 years old and has survived arson attempts, and a wooden door now closes the hollow. Do not go looking for the door on the Ashcombe tree; it belongs to the other one, and our pin does not mark it separately. Treat the pair as one visit.

Nobody has published a girth or a height for the Ashcombe chestnut, and the 'before 1700' date comes from that single map record, so read the age as three or four centuries and loosely held. If you have measured either tree, tell us.

The most recent record we have of it standing is an OpenStreetMap edit from May 2024. If you visit, tell us how both trees look.

Carshalton Park is free and open, about 10 minutes' walk from Carshalton station.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the old sweet chestnut at the Ashcombe Road edge of the park, one of its group of veteran chestnuts. It stands about 60 metres from the second Great Tree, the chestnut with a door in its hollow.

trees.story:
In 1832 a visitor named Glynne, writing up St Mary's church in Downe, called its yew 'a very fine yew'. A church note published by the Kent Archaeological Society goes further and records 'one very ancient Yew tree to the south of the church porch'. It is still there, in the churchyard of the village where Charles Darwin made his home at Down House.

What neither note gives is a number. Nobody has published a measured girth or a dated age for this tree. Bigger claims for both circulate online, but none we have found comes with a source we trust, so we leave the age blank rather than borrow one. If you know of a measurement, or you have one, tell us.

What we can say is that it was one of the original 41 Great Trees of London, the list Trees for Cities drew up of the capital's remarkable trees, and that it appears to be alive. A naturalist's record from October 2025, made close by, may well be this tree. Downe looks like a Kent village and feels a long way from London, but it sits inside the London Borough of Bromley, which is how a country churchyard yew ends up on a list of the city's trees.

The churchyard is free and open to visitors. There is no station in the village. Take a train to Orpington or Bromley South and a local bus from there, and combine it with Down House, a short walk away.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the ancient yew just south of the church porch. It stands in the churchyard of St Mary the Virgin, Downe.
